problem.summary: 传统计算机视觉和机器学习方法在手写数字识别、交通标志识别等任务上无法达到人类水平性能。

motivation.summary: 受生物视觉系统启发，通过构建深度、宽的卷积神经网络架构来提升图像分类性能，特别是利用多列DNN（MCDNN）集成不同预处理输入的预测。

core_idea.summary: 提出多列深度神经网络（MCDNN），每列DNN是深度卷积网络，使用小感受野和最大池化实现深度结构，仅训练获胜神经元；多列DNN对不同预处理输入的预测进行平均，以提升分类准确性和鲁棒性。

method.summary: 构建深度卷积神经网络（DNN）架构，使用小卷积核和最大池化层；采用在线梯度下降训练，仅更新获胜神经元的权重；通过数据增强（平移、缩放、旋转、弹性变形）和多种预处理（如直方图均衡化、对比度归一化）生成不同输入；组合多个DNN列形成MCDNN，对各列预测进行民主平均。

experiments.summary: 在MNIST手写数字、NIST SD 19拉丁字符、CASIA中文字符、GTSRB交通标志、CIFAR10自然图像和NORB 3D玩具等多个基准数据集上进行实验，评估MCDNN的分类错误率，并与现有最佳方法比较。

claims.claim: MCDNN在MNIST上首次达到接近人类水平的性能（错误率0.23%）。
MCDNN在交通标志识别基准上以两倍优势超越人类。
MCDNN在多个常见图像分类基准上提升了现有最佳水平。
多列集成和不同预处理能有效降低错误率。
GPU实现使得大规模深度网络训练可行。

limitations.limitation: 论文未详细讨论模型的计算复杂度和内存需求；MCDNN需要训练多个DNN列，训练时间较长；对于某些数据集（如中文字符），训练数据量巨大，对计算资源要求高；方法主要针对图像分类任务，未扩展到其他计算机视觉任务。

nodes.title: 深度卷积神经网络（DNN）架构
nodes.label: DNN Architecture
nodes.summary: 构建深度卷积神经网络，使用小卷积核和最大池化层，实现类似哺乳动物视觉皮层的层次结构。
nodes.description: DNN由多个卷积层、最大池化层和全连接层堆叠而成。卷积层使用小卷积核（如2x2、3x3），最大池化层通过局部抑制选择获胜神经元，实现下采样。网络深度可达6-10层，顶层为标准多层感知器（MLP）。

nodes.title: 获胜神经元训练
nodes.label: Winner-Take-All Training
nodes.summary: 仅训练获胜神经元，减少突触变化，降低能耗，符合生物合理性。
nodes.description: 在最大池化层中，只有获胜神经元（即局部区域内最活跃的神经元）被训练，其他神经元不更新权重。这减少了权重更新次数，降低了能量消耗，并防止非获胜神经元遗忘已学知识。

nodes.title: 多列DNN（MCDNN）集成
nodes.label: Multi-column DNN Ensemble
nodes.summary: 组合多个DNN列，每列处理不同预处理输入，通过平均预测提升性能。
nodes.description: MCDNN由多个DNN列组成，每列可以独立训练在相同或不同预处理的输入上。在测试时，对所有列的预测进行民主平均，得到最终分类结果。这类似于大脑皮层微柱结构。

nodes.title: 数据增强与预处理
nodes.label: Data Augmentation and Preprocessing
nodes.summary: 通过平移、缩放、旋转、弹性变形等增强训练数据，并使用多种预处理方法生成不同输入视图。
nodes.description: 训练时，图像在每个epoch前进行随机平移、缩放、旋转和弹性变形（针对字符）。此外，使用多种预处理方法（如直方图均衡化、自适应直方图均衡化、对比度归一化）生成不同输入，用于训练不同DNN列。

nodes.title: 在线梯度下降训练
nodes.label: Online Gradient Descent Training
nodes.summary: 使用在线梯度下降和退火学习率训练DNN，权重随机初始化。
nodes.description: DNN使用在线梯度下降训练，即每个样本后更新权重。学习率从初始值（如0.001）按因子（如0.993/epoch）退火，直到达到最小值（如0.00003）。权重从均匀随机分布初始化。

nodes.title: GPU加速训练
nodes.label: GPU-Accelerated Training
nodes.summary: 利用图形处理器（GPU）实现快速训练，处理大规模数据集。
nodes.description: GPU实现使得大规模深度网络训练可行，例如在中文字符数据集上，CPU训练需数天，而GPU训练大幅缩短时间。

glossary.MCDNN: 多列深度神经网络，由多个DNN列组成，每列处理不同预处理输入，预测平均。
glossary.DNN: 深度神经网络，本文特指深度卷积神经网络。
glossary.Winner-Take-All: 获胜者全得，指最大池化中仅获胜神经元被训练的机制。
glossary.Max Pooling: 最大池化，通过局部区域选择最大激活值实现下采样。
glossary.Data Augmentation: 数据增强，通过变换（如平移、旋转）增加训练数据多样性。
glossary.Preprocessing: 预处理，如直方图均衡化、对比度归一化，用于生成不同输入视图。
glossary.Online Gradient Descent: 在线梯度下降，每个样本后更新权重。
glossary.Annealed Learning Rate: 退火学习率，学习率随训练逐渐减小。
glossary.GPU: 图形处理器，用于加速矩阵运算和网络训练。
glossary.Confusion Matrix: 混淆矩阵，显示分类错误分布。

required_models: 深度卷积神经网络（DNN）架构，具体层配置见论文描述（如2x48x48-100C5-MP2-100C5-MP2-100C4-MP2-300N-100N-6N）
required_compute: GPU（用于加速训练，具体型号未指定，但需支持CUDA）
足够内存处理大规模数据集（如中文字符数据集3GB）

steps.description: 1. 准备数据集，下载并预处理（如归一化、裁剪）。
2. 实现DNN架构，包括卷积层、最大池化层、全连接层，使用缩放双曲正切和softmax激活函数。
3. 实现数据增强：训练时随机平移、缩放、旋转、弹性变形（针对字符）。
4. 实现多种预处理方法（如直方图均衡化、自适应直方图均衡化、对比度归一化）。
5. 训练多个DNN列，每列使用不同预处理输入或相同输入但不同随机初始化。
6. 实现在线梯度下降训练，使用退火学习率（如初始0.001，因子0.993/epoch，最小0.00003）。
7. 实现MCDNN集成：测试时平均所有DNN列的预测概率。
8. 在验证集上监控错误率，训练至验证错误为零或学习率达最小值。
9. 评估在测试集上的错误率，并与论文结果比较。

metadata.title: Multi-column deep neural networks for image classification
metadata.venue: 2012 IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition
metadata.paper_type: Computer Vision / CNN / Computer Vision / Top-cited Computer Vision paper
metadata.abstract: Traditional methods of computer vision and machine learning cannot match human performance on tasks such as the recognition of handwritten digits or traffic signs. Our biologically plausible, wide and deep artificial neural network architectures can. Small (often minimal) receptive fields of convolutional winner-take-all neurons yield large network depth, resulting in roughly as many sparsely connected neural layers as found in mammals between retina and visual cortex. Only winner neurons are trained. Several deep neural columns become experts on inputs preprocessed in different ways; their predictions are averaged. Graphics cards allow for fast training. On the very competitive MNIST handwriting benchmark, our method is the first to achieve near-human performance. On a traffic sign recognition benchmark it outperforms humans by a factor of two. We also improve the state-of-the-art on a plethora of common image classification benchmarks.

anchors.text_span: Multi-column Deep Neural Networks for Image Classiﬁcation Dan Cires ¸an Ueli Meier J¨urgen Schmidhuber Technical Report No. IDSIA-04-12 February 2012 IDSIA / USI-SUPSI Dalle Molle Institute for Artiﬁcial Intelligence Galleria 2, 6928 Manno, Switzerland IDSIA is a joint institute of both University of Lugano (USI) and University of Applied Sciences of Southern Switzerland (SUPSI), and was founded in 1988 by the Dalle Molle Foundation which promoted quality of life. arXiv:1202.2745v1 [cs.CV] 13 Feb 2012
Technical Report No. IDSIA-04-12 1 Multi-column Deep Neural Networks for Image Classiﬁcation Dan Cires ¸an Ueli Meier J¨urgen Schmidhuber February 2012
Abstract
Traditional methods of computer vision and machine learning cannot match human performance on
tasks such as the recognition of handwritten digits or trafﬁc signs. Our biologically plausible deep arti-
ﬁcial neural network architectures can. Small (often minimal) receptive ﬁelds of convolutional winner-
take-all neurons yield large network depth, resulting in roughly as many sparsely connected neural layers

as found in mammals between retina and visual cortex. Only winner neurons are trained. Several deep neural columns become experts on inputs preprocessed in different ways; their predictions are averaged. Graphics cards allow for fast training. On the very competitive MNIST handwriting benchmark, our method is the ﬁrst to achieve near-human performance. On a trafﬁc sign recognition benchmark it out- performs humans by a factor of two. We also improve the state-of-the-art on a plethora of common image classiﬁcation benchmarks.
1 Introduction

Recent publications suggest that unsupervised pre-training of deep, hierarchical neural networks improves supervised pattern classiﬁcation [2, 10]. Here we train such nets by simple online back-propagation, setting new, greatly improved records on MNIST [20], Latin letters [13], Chinese characters [23], trafﬁc signs [36], NORB (jittered, cluttered) [21] and CIFAR10 [18] benchmarks. We focus on deep convolutional neural networks (DNN), introduced by [11], improved by [20], reﬁned and simpliﬁed by [1, 35, 7]. Lately, DNN proved their mettle on data sets ranging from handwritten digits (MNIST) [5, 7], handwritten characters [6] to 3D toys (NORB) and faces [37]. DNNs fully unfold their potential when they are big and deep [7]. But training them requires weeks, months, even years on CPUs. High data transfer latency prevents multi-threading and multi-CPU code from saving the situation. 2 Architecture
The initially random weights of the DNN are iteratively trained to minimize the classiﬁcation error on a set

of labeled training images; generalization performance is then tested on a separate set of test images. Our architecture does this by combining several techniques in a novel way: (1) Unlike the shallow NN used in many 1990s applications, ours are deep, inspired by the Neocogni- tron [11], with many (6-10) layers of non-linear neurons stacked on top of each other, comparable to the number of layers found between retina and visual cortex of macaque monkeys [3]. (2) It was shown [14] that such multi-layered DNN are hard to train by standard gradient descent [39, 19, 30], the method of choice from a mathematical/algorithmic point of view. Today’s computers, however, are fast enough for this, more than 60000 times faster than those of the early 90s 1. Carefully designed code for massively parallel graphics processing units (GPUs normally used for video games) allows for gaining an additional speedup factor of 50-100 over serial code for standard computers. Given enough labeled data, our ne...
max pooling technique [29] determines winning neurons by partitioning layers into quadratic regions of

local inhibition, selecting the most active neuron of each region. The winners of some layer represent a smaller, down-sampled layer with lower resolution, feeding the next layer in the hierarchy. The approach
is inspired by Hubel and Wiesel’s seminal work on the cat’s primary visual cortex [40], which identi-
ﬁed orientation-selectivesimple cells with overlapping local receptive ﬁelds andcomplex cells performing

down-sampling-like operations [15]. (4) Note that at some point down-sampling automatically leads to the ﬁrst 1-dimensional layer. From then on, only trivial 1-dimensional winner-take-all regions are possible, that is, the top part of the hierarchy becomes a standard multi-layer perceptron (MLP) [39, 19, 30]. Receptive ﬁelds and winner-take-all regions
of our DNN often are (near-)minimal, e.g., only 2x2 or 3x3 neurons. This results in (near-)maximal depth
of layers with non-trivial (2-dimensional) winner-take-all regions. In fact, insisting on minimal 2x2 ﬁelds

automatically deﬁnes the entire deep architecture, apart from the number of different convolutional kernels per layer [20, 1, 35, 7] and the depth of the plain MLP on top. (5) Only winner neurons are trained, that is, other neurons cannot forget what they learnt so far, although they may be affected by weight changes in more peripheral layers. The resulting decrease of synaptic
changes per time interval corresponds to biologically plausible reduction of energy consumption. Our

training algorithm is fully online, i.e. weight updates occur after each gradient computation step. (6) Inspired by microcolumns of neurons in the cerebral cortex, we combine several DNN columns to form a Multi-column DNN (MCDNN). Given some input pattern, the predictions of all columns are democratically averaged. Before training, the weights (synapses) of all columns are randomly initialized. Various columns can be trained on the same inputs, or on inputs preprocessed in different ways. The latter helps to reduce both error rate and number of columns required to reach a given accuracy. The MCDNN architecture and its training and testing procedures are illustrated in Figure 1.

3.3 Chinese characters
Compared to Latin character recognition, isolated Chinese character recognition is a much harder problem,
mainly because of the much larger category set, but also because of wide variability of writing styles, and

the confusion between similar characters. We use a dataset from the Institute of Automation of Chinese Academy of Sciences (CASIA [23]), which contains 300 samples for each of 3755 characters (in GB1 set). This resulted in a data set with more than 1 Million characters (3GB of data) which posed a major computational challenge even to our system. Without our fast GPU implementation the nets on this task would train for more than one year. Only the forward propagation of the training set takes 27h on a normal CPU, and training a single epoch would consequently have lasted several days. On our fast GPU implementation on the other hand, training a single epoch takes 3.4h, which makes it feasible to train a net within a few days instead of many months. We train following DNN, 1x48x48-100C3-MP2-200C2-MP2-300C2-MP2-400C2-MP2-500N-3755N, on ofﬂine as well as on online characters. For the ofﬂine character recognition task, we resize all characters

As suggested by the organizers, the ﬁrst 240 writers from the database CASIA-HWDB1.1 are used for training and the remaining 60 writers are used for testing. 3.6 NORB

We test a MCDNN with four columns on NORB (jittered-cluttered) [21], a collection of stereo images of 3D models (Figure 5). The objects are centrally placed on randomly chosen backgrounds, and there is also cluttering from a peripherally placed second object. This database is designed for experimenting with 3D object recognition from shape. It contains images of 50 toys belonging to 5 generic categories: four-legged animals, human ﬁgures, airplanes, trucks, and cars. The objects were imaged by two cameras under 6 lighting conditions, 9 elevations (30 to 70 degrees every 5 degrees), and 18 azimuths (0 to 340 every 20 degrees). The training set has 10 folds of 29160 images each for a total of 291600 images; the testing set consists of two folds totalizing 58320 images.

4 Conclusion

This is the ﬁrst time human-competitive results are reported on widely used computer vision benchmarks. On many other image classiﬁcation datasets our MCDNN improves the state-of-the-art by 30-80% (Tab. 7). We drastically improve recognition rates on MNIST, NIST SD 19, Chinese characters, trafﬁc signs, CI-

Technical Report No. IDSIA-04-12 11 FAR10 and NORB. Our method is fully supervised and does not use any additional unlabeled data source. Single DNN already are sufﬁcient to obtain new state-of-the-art results; combining them into MCDNNs yields further dramatic performance boosts.

• Histogram Equalization (Histeq) enhances contrast by transforming pixel intensities such that the

output image histogram is roughly uniform [24]. • Adaptive Histogram Equalization (Adapthisteq) operates (unlike Histeq) on tiles rather than the entire image, we tiled the image in 8 nonoverlapping regions of 6x6 pixels. Each tile’s contrast is enhanced such that its histogram becomes roughly uniform [24].

Note that the above normalizations, except Conorm, are performed in a color space with image intensity as one of its components. For this purpose we transform the image from RGB- to Lab-space, then perform normalization, then transform the result back to RGB-space.
